reason: The text presents a nuanced portrayal of elite figures rather than uniformly unfavorable treatment. The tribal leaders and elders of Israel (כָּל־ שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל and זִקְנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל) are portrayed favorably—they recognize David's legitimacy as king and make a covenant with him. Hiram, king of Tyre, is portrayed neutrally to positively, sending craftsmen and materials to build David's house. While some elite figures are portrayed unfavorably (Michal despises David; the Jebusites are defeated as enemies; the Philistines are portrayed as hostile adversaries), the text does not uniformly portray the elite unfavorably. The portrayal is contextual: those who support David are favorable, while those who oppose him are presented as obstacles. The dominant elite figures in the narrative—the Israeli tribal leaders—are decidedly favorable.
